name: Ruy López Chigorin Variation
summary: The Chigorin Variation of the Closed Ruy López plays 9...Na5 to kick the bishop and expand on the queenside with ...c5 and ...Qc7.
intro: The Chigorin Variation is the classical main line of the Closed Ruy López, reached after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 a6 4.Ba4 Nf6 5.O-O Be7 6.Re1 b5 7.Bb3 d6 8.c3 O-O 9.h3 Na5 10.Bc2 c5 11.d4 Qc7. Its signature move is 9...Na5, immediately harassing the strong b3-bishop and forcing it back to c2, after which Black rolls forward on the queenside with ...c5 and supports the centre with ...Qc7. For much of the twentieth century this was regarded as the main line of the entire Spanish, a battleground where generations of grandmasters tested the balance between Black's queenside expansion and the slightly awkward placement of the knight on the rim.

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The Chigorin is built on a clear-cut plan: with 9...Na5 Black removes White's dangerous light-squared bishop from the a2-g8 diagonal, driving it to the more passive c2-square, and then seizes queenside space with ...c5. The pawn on c5 strikes at White's d4-point and, together with ...Qc7 and the half-open c-file, gives Black concrete counterplay on that wing. The queen on c7 supports both the e5-pawn and the c5-pawn while eyeing the c-file, making it a natural hub for Black's queenside operations. This gives the Chigorin a more committal, plan-driven character than the flexible manoeuvring systems of the Spanish.

The trade-off is the knight on a5, which sits on the edge of the board far from the kingside. If Black cannot bring it back into play, it can become a chronic liability, and a recurring theme is the manoeuvre ...Nc6 or ...Nc4 (after a later ...c4) to reactivate it. In return, the knight does useful work pressuring White's centre and clearing c6 for the queen and pawns. The central tension between White's d4 and Black's e5 and c5 pawns is the defining strategic feature: whoever resolves it on favourable terms usually dictates the middlegame, and both sides invest great care in the timing of d4-d5, ...cxd4, and ...c4.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: After 11.d4 Qc7 the position is a classic closed-centre Spanish tabiya. White's principal choices are to maintain the tension, to close with d5, or to invite exchanges with dxe5, each leading to a distinct type of game. A major branch is 12.Nbd2, developing and preparing Nf1-g3 or Nf1-e3, when Black continues ...Nc6 or ...cxd4 followed by piece play against the centre. The classical 12.d5 gains space and steers toward a manoeuvring struggle where Black seeks the ...c4 break and knight reroute, while White expands on the kingside.

Black has several move-order treatments of the same plan, and closely related systems include lines where Black delays ...Qc7 in favour of ...Nc6 or ...Bd7. The Chigorin dominated top-level Ruy López practice for decades and provided the theoretical backdrop against which the rival Breyer and Zaitsev systems were later developed. Although the ...Na5 plan has since ceded some popularity to those setups, which keep the knight better placed, the Chigorin remains fully respectable and a frequent visitor at every level, prized for the clarity of its queenside counterplay.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The variation is named after Mikhail Chigorin, the great Russian master of the late nineteenth century and a founding figure of the Russian and Soviet chess schools. Chigorin was a lifelong champion of active piece play and dynamic counterattack, and his handling of the Ruy López did much to shape the classical understanding of the opening. The ...Na5 and ...c5 plan bearing his name became the standard way to meet the Closed Spanish and anchored elite opening theory for the better part of a century.

It should not be confused with the Chigorin Defence to the Queen's Gambit (1.d4 d5 2.c4 Nc6), another idea named after the same player. In the Ruy López the Chigorin was a workhorse of World Championship matches and top tournaments through much of the twentieth century before the Breyer and Zaitsev variations offered players a way to keep the knight more actively placed. Even so, its direct, understandable strategy makes it an enduring teaching example of queenside expansion against a closed centre, and it retains a loyal following.
